what_it_does: When a large web application handles millions of requests, it records detailed traces — step-by-step logs showing how each request traveled through the system — to help engineers diagnose slowdowns. Storing every trace in full is prohibitively expensive, so systems typically keep only a random sample, discarding the rest entirely. Mint takes a different approach: instead of the all-or-nothing sampling choice, it recognizes that most requests follow the same structural pattern (the same sequence of services), and stores that common skeleton just once. For each individual request, it stores only the small differences from the skeleton — the deviations in timing, errors, or unusual paths. This way, all requests are represented, storage costs drop substantially, and engineers can still reconstruct the full picture for any request.
